records.title: The legacy branches of GET /api/organizations/tree and POST /api/organizations/switch fill missing values with invented ones: in both a null created_at or updated_at is replaced by the time of the request and a null type becomes union, and the tree also turns a null status into active, a null hierarchy level into 0 and a null member count into 0, so the caller reads a creation date, a type, a lifecycle status and a size that the organization record does not hold.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The tree read is bounded to the organizations the caller may read, ordered and limited (upstream), and now runs as the system role like the hierarchy route instead of the ambient connection role.

records.title: In the legacy mode POST /api/organizations/switch accepts any organization_members row of the user and the organization as the membership (it reads neither the status nor the removal flag of the row, and does not check that the organization is active), so a suspended, inactive or removed member and a member of an archived organization receive success true together with the organization name, slug, type, parent id, sector, jurisdiction and description, although the organization resolver that later reads the selection cookie requires an active, non-removed membership; an identifier on the PLATFORM_ADMIN_USER_IDS environment list switches to any organization without any membership; and the route stores nothing server side (the client then writes the selection into cookies it controls), so success true reports a validation and not a switch.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: A legacy organization switch needs an active, non-removed membership of an active organization (B21 implementation, pinned by the F07 contract test).

records.title: POST /api/organizations/switch changes the organization a session works in (the canonical mode revokes the active session and issues a new session row bound to the chosen organization, or writes a provider preference cookie) and neither the route, the canonical selection handler nor rebindSessionOrganization writes an audit record of who selected which organization from which, so the selection of an organization, including a platform administrator selecting an organization they hold no membership of in the legacy mode, leaves no audit trail and the mutation of the session store is not atomic with any audit record.

GET /api/organizations/platform-id returns the constant DEFAULT_ORGANIZATION_ID of the source file as platformOrgId without reading the organizations table: the constant is documented in organization-utils as the Default Organization where all users start (the organization that the non-production fallback assigns to a user with no membership), not as the organization of type platform, so a client that distinguishes viewing the platform from viewing a tenant (the sidebar compares the organization id with this same constant) treats the default tenant organization as the platform, and every signed-in user receives the internal identifier of that organization.

GET /api/platform/metrics/mrr, GET /api/platform/metrics/churn and GET /api/platform/metrics/unit-economics are three copies of one handler that ignores the request, reads no table and returns the fixed object activeUsers 0, requestsToday 0, errorRate 0 under the OpenAPI summary System metrics: a caller that asks for monthly recurring revenue, churn or unit economics receives zeros for three system-usage keys that are none of those figures (no mrr, churn or unit-economics key exists), presented with HTTP 200 as aggregated system metrics, although the subscription event, MRR snapshot and customer acquisition tables exist in the financial service schema and no route under app/api reads them.

currentRun.repair: Removed fixed HTTP 200 usage counters from three platform financial metric routes; system-admin authentication and explicit private no-store HTTP 501 until actual MRR/churn/unit-economics sources and platform authority are qualified.
currentRun.limits: Containment only. Financial metrics calculation, reconciliation, authority mandate, PostgreSQL and real HTTP acceptance remain unimplemented/unverified. No zero or outcome is claimed.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The three platform financial metrics answer 501 with a NOT_IMPLEMENTED capability state and no figures (existing implementation and test).

records.title: The three platform metric routes under /api/platform/metrics are gated at the admin role floor (the organization administrator level of ROLE_HIERARCHY, 140) while the other platform-wide reads (the platform statistics and the platform operator routes) use the platform_lead floor (270): a route of the platform namespace that is wired to the platform revenue tables (mrr_snapshots has no organization column and subscription_events holds the events of every organization) would hand platform-wide revenue and churn aggregates to the administrator of every organization, and the route is a role-title check with no platform-staff mandate.

GET /api/platform/stats admits any caller whose role title is platform_lead or above (a role-title floor, not an issued platform-staff mandate) and returns, for every organization other than the platform type, an organization list with name, type, status, member and active member counts, sectors, CLC affiliation, subscription tier and per-capita rate, together with registered and active user counts, role distribution, grievance, collective agreement and settlement counts, the total monetary value of all settlements and the sector breakdown: the statements run on the shared db client with no organization predicate, no withSystemContext and no withRLSContext (so whether they see every tenant depends on the connection role) and the read is not audited.

The figures of GET /api/platform/stats are named for something other than what is computed: registeredUsers is the count of organization_members rows (one person with several memberships counts several times and removed members are not excluded) and activeUsers is the count of rows whose status is active, totalMonetaryValue is the sum of the integer monetary_amount of every settlement in every status (proposed and rejected settlements included, in no stated currency), and resolved grievances are only those with status settled; the dashboard shows these under labels of users, settlement value and resolved cases, so a count of rows and a sum of unaccepted amounts read as measured facts.

GET /api/portal/dues/balance reads the organization id from the organizationId query value or the x-organization-id header and queries member_dues_ledger through the shared db import with the session user id and that organization id as its only predicates: it does not verify that the caller is a member of the named organization (the sibling pay GET does), opens no withRLSContext, and returns totals and the last five entries, so the answer is bounded only by the user id predicate and by whatever row-level-security the connection role enforces.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The balance reads the authenticated member and organization from the session only and never fabricates a balance when there is no ledger activity; upstream's change, covered by an existing test.

records.title: The balanceStatus of GET /api/portal/dues/balance is computed as currentBalance <= 0 ? paid_up : currentBalance > 0 ? owing : credit, so the credit branch can never be returned: a member whose balance is negative (overpaid) is reported as paid_up and the credit they hold is not distinguished from a zero balance.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: A credit balance is reported when posted payments exceed posted charges; upstream's change, covered by an existing test.

records.title: GET /api/portal/dues/pay is described as the member payment history but selects every transaction type of the member dues ledger (charges, credits, adjustments, write-offs and payments) under the key payments, includes the processor payment reference and receipt number, never lists the pending dues_transactions attempts that POST creates, and takes the page size from parseInt of the query value, so a non-numeric limit becomes NaN and the query limit is undefined.

POST /api/portal/dues/pay computes the outstanding balance, inserts a new pending dues_transactions row for the whole balance and creates a Stripe PaymentIntent with an idempotency key derived from that new row id, without looking for an existing pending payment of the member, so every call creates another full-balance intent; the settlement path locks and settles only the paid row and credits member_dues_ledger by that row amount (balance_after is the prior balance minus the amount, with no floor and no comparison with the balance owed), so two confirmed intents credit the ledger twice.

records.title: POST /api/portal/dues/pay commits the pending dues_transactions row and its dues.payment_initiated audit row in one transaction and only then calls the Stripe API outside any transaction; the later update that stores processor_payment_id and the update that sets the row to cancelled after a processor failure are separate transactions with no audit row, and the cancellation is wrapped in a catch that discards its own failure, so an initiation can be audited for a payment whose provider call never happened and the cancelled state is not audited.

POST /api/portal/dues/pay sends the organization id and the member user id in the PaymentIntent metadata to Stripe through the platform-managed Stripe client (lib/stripe delegates to a platform client; the route holds no per-organization processor configuration): no source names the merchant account that receives union dues, whether it is the union or the platform operator, or the member consent for the disclosure, and the route holds no per-organization processor configuration.

The generic CRUD routes at /api/precedents/[id] are configured orgScoped true over arbitration_precedents, whose organization column is named source_organization_id and which has no organizationId, no status and no userId or memberId: the factory adds the tenant predicate only for an organizationId column and the low-role guard holds a caller to own rows only for a userId or memberId column, so GET (member), PATCH (steward) and DELETE (administrator) address any precedent row of any organization by id, whatever its sharing_level and shared_with_org_ids.

remaining: Cross-organization sharing of precedents is unavailable: union_eyes_system has no privilege on arbitration_precedents and the deployed policy is owner-only. A reviewed multi-party policy migration is required to restore it.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The precedent item route reads under the caller's tenant context with an explicit sharing check, and PATCH and DELETE name the owning organization in their own WHERE clause and audit in the same transaction (existing implementation, existing pglite isolation test).

records.title: PATCH /api/precedents/[id] copies the request body into the arbitration_precedents update, so a steward can change sharing_level, shared_with_org_ids, is_parties_anonymized (turning the anonymization of the parties off), the document links and the source_organization_id itself with no sharing authority, no review and no record of the previous value; the audit row lists only the changed field names.

DELETE /api/precedents/[id] permanently deletes the arbitration_precedents row (the table has no status column, so the factory hard-deletes) and the foreign keys on precedent_tags and precedent_citations cascade, so the tags and the citation history of the precedent are destroyed with no soft delete, no withdrawal rule and an audit row that keeps only the row id and the changed field names.

GET /api/precedents (list, issue type, most cited) and POST /api/precedents/search select every column of arbitration_decisions at the member and steward floor, including the grievor name, the panel members, the full text and the embedding, and apply no condition on is_public or access_restrictions, so a decision recorded as not public or carrying an access restriction is returned and searched (the search also matches inside the full text) exactly like a public one; the table has no organization column and the library is shared across organizations.

GET /api/precedents passes parseInt of the limit and page query values to the list, most-cited and issue-type queries with no maximum, no minimum and no NaN check, so a caller can request an arbitrarily large page, a negative offset or a NaN limit, and the sortBy value is taken from the query string; the statistics mode counts the whole library.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The precedent collection refuses an invalid page or a limit above 100 with 400 (existing implementation and tests).

records.title: POST /api/precedents/search validates only that the query is a string of at most 500 characters and that filters is a record of unknown values, then builds %query% LIKE conditions over the title, case number, summary, headnote and full text without escaping the percent and underscore wildcards, and casts the filter values to the tribunal and precedent value enums without validating them, so an invalid enum value reaches the database as a 500 and a broad pattern scans the whole text column.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Search terms take the LIKE wildcards literally, the search accepts only the two filters it reads (strict, bounded lists), and a filter value outside the column's declared values is refused with 400 instead of reaching the database as a 500. The same service also excludes decisions marked not public or restricted.

records.title: POST /api/precedents inserts the typed decision into the library that every organization reads, with the full text, grievor and parties as typed, is_public defaulting to true, no source or import provenance and no organization on the row (the organization appears only in the audit row), after a single role-title check (content_manager) and with no review, redaction or consent step.

PUT /api/precedents/jurisdiction-preferences selects the caller row and then updates or inserts it, but member_jurisdiction_preferences declares no unique index on user_id and organization_id, so two concurrent first saves insert two rows and GET returns an arbitrary one of them; includeNational and autoApply are written as typed with no boolean check, and no precedent route reads the preferences (only the console components apply them in the browser), so the saved preference filters nothing on the server.

GET /api/profile/roles is the generic CRUD list over the profiles table (readRole member, orgScoped true) although profiles has no organization column, so the tenant predicate is not added, and the low-role guard restricts only callers below steward to their own row: a steward or higher of any organization receives every profile of the platform with email, membership tier, payment provider, Stripe customer and subscription ids, Whop ids, plan dates and credit counters.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The route returns only the caller's own live roles; it is no longer the generic factory over the unscoped profiles table (upstream's change, existing test).

records.title: The route named profile/roles lists billing profiles (membership tier, payment provider and credits) and holds no role, role assignment or permission data, so a client that expects a role list receives subscription records; its POST is configured at the steward floor but profiles is READ_ONLY in the CRUD governance table, so every POST is refused with 403 after the role check, and no route assigns a role.

GET /api/profile/me returns isSuccess true with the message Profile retrieved successfully and data null when the profile query fails or times out: getProfileByUserId catches the lookup error and returns null, so a database failure and a user who has no profile are indistinguishable from each other, and the caller is told the profile was retrieved.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: A new strict lookup throws on a failed or timed-out query (and clears its timer); the profile route answers that as a failure, and says no profile exists only when the lookup completed and found none. The tolerant lookup remains for callers that treat failure as no profile.

records.title: GET /api/reconciliation/process?runId= checks the caller finance:view mandate in the caller own organization and then returns getReconciliationRun(runId), whose query is .where(eq(reconciliationRuns.id, runId)) with no organization condition and which is read through the shared db handle, so an officer of any organization with the commercial_reporting entitlement reads any other organization reconciliation run (totals, variance, counts, run-by user, billing period) by id.

unitOrSourceEvidence: db/__tests__/tenant-isolation-remediation.postgres.test.ts (reconciliation run lookup, run on a connection where RLS does not apply)

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The run lookup is bound to the caller's organization (another organization's run reads as not found); upstream's change, covered by an existing test.

records.title: The reconciliation service (runReconciliation, resolveException, getReconciliationRun, listExceptions, requireReconciliation) imports the shared db handle and opens its own db.transaction without a tenant context, so the organization predicates written in each query (and absent from getReconciliationRun and requireReconciliation) are the only boundary unless the connection role is itself subject to row-level security, which the route files do not establish; the mandate check in the route runs in a separate withRLSContext transaction that the service does not join.

runReconciliation writes the run, matches and exceptions in db.transaction but calls auditLog (the application audit logger, which does not take the transaction handle) inside it, and resolveException updates the exception and then calls auditLog after the update committed, so the audit event is a separate write: a failed audit of a resolution or write-off leaves the status changed without the record (and in legacy mode the logger logs and swallows a database failure), and a run that later rolls back can leave its audit event behind.

POST /api/reconciliation/process inserts a new reconciliation_runs row and fresh exception rows on every call for the same period (no uniqueness, no supersede or correction of an earlier run), stores the billingPeriodId from the body without checking that the period belongs to the organization, and requireReconciliation(billingPeriodId), the guard that decides whether a period may be closed, filters the runs by period id alone with limit 1 and no order, so a run of one organization (or any earlier run) can satisfy the closure guard; the only caller of that guard is closeBillingPeriod, which no route calls.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: For an organization run, the period is locked, a billing period named in the request must be the organization's own (404), and a second run for the same period is refused (409, naming the earlier run) instead of adding a second set of exceptions. A period that ends before it starts is refused. The existing mocked test of a run gained the two new checks in its queue; three tests were added.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: The service still accepts a run with no organization, which reconciles every organization together; no route uses that mode, but it is not removed.

records.title: runReconciliation records a fee_settlement match for each fee event that has a settlement batch id by copying the fee amount as both the source and the target amount with a variance of 0.00, without reading any settlement batch amount, so these matches are always reported as matched; it sums payments whose status is refunded into the payment total as if received; and the exception types duplicate_payment, missing_fee_event and orphaned_refund that the schema defines are never created, so the run reports totals and exception counts that do not test duplicates, missing fees or refunds.

POST /api/reconciliation/resolve sets an exception to resolved or written_off with the typed notes (an empty string is accepted) and the resolver id, and changes no invoice, payment or ledger row, so a write-off removes the exception from the open list without any financial effect or evidence; the service does not compare the resolver with the user who ran the reconciliation, no second approver is required, and the mandate check passes no participants to the segregation-of-duties rule.

GET /api/reconciliation/bank lists the reconciliation runs of the organization and GET /api/reconciliation/upload lists reconciliation exceptions; neither receives, parses or matches a bank statement (the upload route comment says the intake is reserved for future work), and no route records a bank transaction, so the paths named for bank reconciliation reconcile platform invoices and payments only.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: reconciliation/bank and reconciliation/upload listed runs and exceptions under names promising a bank feed and a file intake; both answer 501 behind the officer floor. The upload route test, which asserted the exception list, was replaced by an assertion of the 501.

records.title: GET /api/reconciliation/bank returns every run of the organization with no limit, and GET /api/reconciliation/upload splits the status query value on commas and casts it to the exception status enum without validation (and returns every matching exception unpaged), so an invalid status value reaches the database as an enum error and the lists grow without bound.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The exception list validates every status against the vocabulary (400 otherwise, before any query), is ordered and bounded at 200. The run list route (reconciliation/bank) answers 501.

records.title: GET /api/rewards/export has no role check: after a session and the organization lookup it selects by organization alone and returns as a CSV download every award (recipient and issuer user ids, reason text), every wallet ledger row (user id, event type, credits, balance, memo) and every budget envelope of the organization to any member, while the wallet and redemption routes hold a member to their own rows.

priorEvidence.nativeEvidence: Partial: tenant-isolation-remediation.postgres.test.ts shows recognition_awards hidden from another organization; the route itself has not run natively.
remaining: Run the export route natively
Institutional decision on the export audience (administrator is an engineering default, not a mandate)

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The export is an administrator's, refuses a member before any query, is audited with the file, bounded and formula-safe (upstream's change, existing test).

records.title: The CSV writer of GET /api/rewards/export quotes only values that contain a comma, a quote or a newline and does not neutralise a leading equals, plus, minus or at sign, so a free-text award reason or ledger memo that begins with a formula is written verbatim and is evaluated when an administrator opens the file in a spreadsheet.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The export neutralises formula cells, is bounded, role-checked and audited in the reading transaction; upstream's change, covered by an existing test.

records.title: GET /api/rewards/export returns the whole awards, ledger or budgets table of the organization in one response with no limit or date range, and records nothing about who exported what: the route writes no audit row and sits under no wrapper that does, so a bulk disclosure of member wallet data leaves no trace.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The export needs the administrator role before any read, is bounded to 5,000 rows, neutralises spreadsheet formula cells, and is audited in the transaction that reads it so a failed audit withholds the file (existing implementation and test).

records.title: The anniversary task of POST /api/rewards/cron selects every organization member whose join date has today month and day and, for each, creates and issues a new Work Anniversary recognition award (credits applied by issueAward) with no check for an award already made for that member and year and no uniqueness on recipient, award type and date in recognition_awards, so the same call repeated on the same day, a scheduler retry or an overlapping run awards and credits the members again; the awards and credits are created in two separate transactions per member.

unitOrSourceEvidence: apps/union-eyes/db/__tests__/rewards-anniversary-concurrency.postgres.test.ts (PG15 and PG16: six overlapping runs award three active members exactly once; with the lock removed the same test records 18 awards)
remaining: A unique index would add a second, schema-level guard; it needs a reviewed migration
E2E through the scheduler

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Repeat protection (an advisory lock per organization and award type, and a same-day NOT EXISTS over the member's awards in any state) was already in the source and is proven on PostgreSQL by anniversary-idempotency.pglite.test.ts (existing, not mine). What was still open is closed here: each member's create and issue is one savepoint, so a failure in either rolls both back and no approved award is left un-issued, one member's failure no longer aborts the others' work in the shared transaction, and the run reports failed members (success false) instead of a smaller count. Proved on PostgreSQL: a failed issue leaves no award for that member and the next run completes only that member.

records.title: The scheduled task of POST /api/rewards/cron loads the active scheduled automation rules of each organization, logs each one and increments processed without evaluating any schedule or issuing any award (the source comment calls it a placeholder), so the response reports rules processed for work that was not done.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: A scheduled rule names an award type and a cron expression but nothing that says who earns the award, so no award can be derived; the task now reports those rules as skipped (and logs a warning) and never as processed. Evaluating scheduled rules remains unbuilt; it is not claimed.

records.title: The expiration task of POST /api/rewards/cron e-mails members whose earn ledger rows have an expires_at inside the next 7, 14 and 30 days (three overlapping windows run on every call, so a row expiring in 5 days is selected in all three), summing the earned credits of those rows and ignoring any spending; the call sites that write earn rows pass no expiresAt and no code was found that writes an expire entry, so today the task selects nothing and reports success with zero notifications, and once an expiry is set it would mail the same member up to three times per run with no sent record and with a credit count that does not reflect what was spent.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The durable sent marker needed no new table: the warning is also the member's in-app notice, recorded in in_app_notifications under data.dedupeKey (unique per organization and member, migration 20261103) before the mail leaves; a second run, retry or overlap mails nothing more, and a failed send releases the record so the next run tries again. Proved on PostgreSQL (PGlite) for repeat, retry-after-failure and per-tier behaviour. The mocked notification-service test now mocks the marker (disclosed).
engineeringCorrection.remaining: Nothing in the product sets an expiry or writes an expire entry yet, so the task still has nothing to warn about until an expiry policy is decided and implemented.

records.title: POST /api/rewards/cron returns success true with HTTP 200 for any task value (an unknown task executes nothing and returns an empty executed list), embeds a per-organization failure as an entry inside a successful response (processAnniversaryAwards returns success false with the error object instead of throwing, and a rejected organization is serialised as an Error object that JSON renders as empty), and wraps the expiration result, whose own success flag may be false, in the same success true, so a scheduler that checks the status code cannot see a failed run.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: An unknown task is a 400 that runs nothing; a rejected organization, an organization that resolves with success false, and an expiration batch whose own flag is false are failures; the run answers 500 naming the scopes; rejected errors serialise as text instead of {}.

records.title: The proxy requires the x-cron-secret header for /api/rewards/cron and compares it with the CRON_SECRET value using !==, and the route then requires the same secret again in an Authorization bearer header (compared in constant time), so a scheduler must send the secret in two transports, a secret query parameter is documented in the route comment but not read, and the GET handler has no secret check of its own and depends on the proxy alone.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The route's own Authorization-only CRON_SECRET-only check is replaced by the shared rule, so one transport (x-cron-secret) satisfies the edge and the route; the edge compare is constant time; the GET handler is removed.

records.title: processAnniversaryAwards computes calculateAnniversaryCredits(yearsOfService) into a variable that is never used (the credit amount issued is the award type default), so a service-based credit scale is implied but not applied, and the reason text stored on every award and shown to the member reads with followed by the organization UUID instead of the organization name.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The unused years-of-service scale and its helper are removed (credits are the award type's configured amount, which issueAward applies); the years are recorded in the award metadata. The reason text names the organization (read inside the transaction) instead of its UUID, tested on PostgreSQL. No years-of-service credit scale is applied: that would be a product decision on money, not a fix.

records.title: The rewards cron route and the wallet, redemption, automation, award and notification services import the shared db handle (and the cron route lists every active organization through it and runs raw SQL on organization_members) without a tenant context, and the wallet and redemption routes are wrapped by withRoleAuth, which sets no row-level-security context, so the organization and user predicates written in each query are the only boundary unless the connection role is itself subject to row-level security, which the route files do not establish.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The cron lists organizations under system authority and runs each organization's anniversary and scheduled task inside that organization's own RLS context, so the services' shared db handle is subject to row-level security on that path.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: The wallet and redemption routes wrapped by withRoleAuth, and the expiration scan (a cross-organization read), still reach the shared handle without a tenant context; each needs its own routing.

records.title: Each anniversary award commits its create audit row in the award transaction and its issue audit row in a second transaction, but the cron run as a whole (organizations covered, members awarded, failures, warnings e-mailed) is written to no audit row, a failure between the two transactions leaves an approved award that is never issued and is not retried, and the expiration e-mails that leave the application are not recorded anywhere beyond a log line.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Each organization's anniversary and scheduled run writes an audit entry (processed, failed or skipped, success) inside its own context, the organizations whose members were e-mailed get an audit entry with the sent and failed counts, an audit that cannot be written fails the run naming the organization, and a member's create and issue are one atomic unit.

records.title: GET /api/rewards/redemptions validates the status query value against pending, ordered, fulfilled, cancelled and refunded (the cancellable states initiated and pending_payment are not in the list) and then never passes it to listUserRedemptions, so the filter has no effect and a member cannot ask for the redemptions that they are allowed to cancel; hasMore is the page length equal to the limit.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The status filter reaches the query (and its total), and the accepted values are the six the redemption status can hold, including the ones a redemption starts in. Two existing assertions adapted for the added argument; new tests cover a valid and an invalid status.

records.title: GET /api/rewards/redemptions returns the whole reward_redemptions row of each of the caller redemptions (listUserRedemptions uses findMany with no column list), including providerPayloadJson, which holds the shop provider checkout payload and the cancellation reason, so provider-side identifiers are returned to the member browser.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The list omits the provider payload and checkout identifier, and a non-numeric or negative page request becomes the bounded default instead of NaN.

records.title: POST /api/rewards/redemptions parses the body with initiateRedemptionSchema into a variable that is never used and then cancels the redemption named by the id query value (refunding the credits), so a client that posts a new redemption receives a cancellation or a missing-id error, the schema validates fields that are ignored, and the cancel does not tell the shop provider that the checkout it may already hold has been cancelled.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The cancel path now validates a cancellation (redemption id and a bounded reason, strict) and uses that validated id; an initiation body is rejected with 400 instead of being parsed and discarded, and the reason is stored with the cancellation. Test updated: the previous cancel test posted an initiation body and a query id, which is the defect.

records.title: GET /api/rewards/wallet reads the balance (the latest ledger row by created_at) and the ledger page in separate statements, so a ledger write between them returns a balance that does not match the page, takes limit and offset from parseInt of the query string without a NaN or negative check, and reports hasMore as the page length equal to the limit.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Limit and offset are parsed to bounded integers (limit 1..100, offset 0..1,000,000), so a non-numeric or negative value is the default rather than NaN or a negative offset; the route reads only the caller own balance and ledger.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: The balance and the ledger are still read in two separate statements, so a movement between them can make them disagree.

records.title: The report definition reads (the collection, the item and every path that is a copy of them) are the generic factory read at a member floor over the reports table: the table has no owner column the factory uses and the routes declare no ownerColumn, so any member of the organization receives every report definition of the organization, including definitions written by other users and definitions whose is_public flag is false, each with its whole config JSON that names data sources, fields and filter values, and no route under /api/reports reads is_public, so the flag restricts nothing.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Report definitions (which sources and filters a report reads) are read at the steward floor, not by any member. No UI consumes these collection routes.

records.title: The report definition writes store the config JSON from the request body as written: the column is an untyped notNull jsonb, no schema bounds its size or depth, and nothing at save time applies the contract of the report executor (a data source id of its registry, registry field ids, its filter operators, its allowed joins) or the allowlist of the execute route, so a definition that names an unknown source, a refused operator or a join to any table is stored and returned as a success that a later run would refuse or misread.

The /api/reports/[id]/execute and /api/reports/[id]/run routes are the same generic crudRoutes configuration over the reports table as the item route: neither imports ReportExecutor, reads a source table or loads the config of the report into an engine, so a GET answers the stored definition row (not a result), a PATCH rewrites the definition (including run_count and last_run_at, which no route ever advances) and answers success, and a DELETE at the administrator floor hard-deletes the report itself, so a caller or client that believes it is running or removing a run removes the report definition.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: reports/[id]/run and reports/[id]/execute were the report item route, so their DELETE removed the report; both answer 501. Ad-hoc execution is POST /api/reports/execute.

records.title: The /api/reports/[id]/share route is the same generic crudRoutes configuration over the reports table as the item route: it has no recipient, link, grant or share column, sends nothing and checks nothing, a PATCH that sets is_public true or false only stores a flag that no route reads, and a DELETE at the administrator floor, the natural verb to revoke a share, hard-deletes the whole report, so a share request is answered with success while nothing is shared, and a revocation destroys the report.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: reports/[id]/share no longer exposes the report table; its DELETE can no longer remove a report. It answers 501 until a recipient grant exists.

records.title: The /api/reports/templates route is the generic collection over the reports table with no template filter: a GET returns every report definition of the organization to any member, including custom, scheduled and private definitions that are not templates (the table has is_template and a template value of report_type and the route reads neither), and a POST stores a definition with is_template false unless the body sets it, so the list that the admin page labels templates is the whole definition table.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The templates route no longer fronts the whole report table: it lists only rows marked as templates with an allow-listed projection, and a create is always stored as an organization template through a strict body schema, in the tenant context and audited.

records.title: The /api/reports/builder and /api/reports/datasources/sample routes are the generic collection over the reports table: the builder answers a GET with the definition rows and a POST stores the posted body as a definition without applying the data source registry or the execute allowlist to it, and the data source sample route, which the data source explorer calls with sourceId and fieldId to preview values, ignores both parameters, reads no data source and returns a page of report definitions under a data key where the explorer reads a samples array, so a field preview is always empty and a POST to the sample route creates a report row.

The /api/reports/scheduled and /api/reports/scheduled/[id] routes are the generic CRUD configuration over the reports table, which has no schedule, recipient, delivery method, export format, next run or active column, while the scheduled report form posts reportId, scheduleType, scheduleConfig, deliveryMethod, recipients, exportFormat and isActive: none of those keys is a column, a create carries neither the notNull name nor the notNull config so it cannot insert a row, a pause or resume PATCH with an action key writes only updated_at and is answered with success, the list answers data and pagination where the page reads schedules, a DELETE hard-deletes a report row, and the scheduled reports cron answers 501, so no schedule, recipient list or delivery exists and the pause, resume and delete the page confirms change nothing about delivery.

POST /api/reports/execute validates the caller-supplied report configuration only for the fields, filters, grouping and sort (the joins are not read by the route) and the executor then builds the join from the caller: any registry table (claims, organization_members, claim_deadlines, dues_assignments) with any registry columns and an operator of =, !=, >, <, >= or <=, the select list qualifies a column with the caller-supplied field.table, and the only organization predicate of the statement is organization_id = the session organization on the base table, so a join such as claims INNER JOIN organization_members ON claims.id != organization_members.id selects id, status and created_at of the member rows of every organization, and claims.id != dues_assignments.id or claim_deadlines does the same for dues assignments and deadlines, up to the executor default limit of 1000 and to any limit the caller names, with whether the rows of other organizations are filtered resting wholly on database row-level security that the route does not set (a tenant transaction and the union_eyes_runtime role exist only when UE_CANONICAL_BOOTSTRAP_V2 is 1).

unitOrSourceEvidence: lib/__tests__/report-executor-tenancy.pglite.test.ts (4 of 6 fail on the previous executor)
db/__tests__/tenant-isolation-remediation.postgres.test.ts (report joins, on a connection where RLS does not apply)
remaining: Same-tenant over-disclosure by report source (institutional decision UE-INST-REPORT-SOURCE-DATA-READERS) is not addressed
Selected fields can only come from the base source's field list

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Every joined table is bound to the caller's organization inside its own ON clause, and a join must follow a declared relationship; proven on real SQL for non-equi, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins (upstream's change, existing test).

records.title: POST /api/reports/execute checks each filter against the route allowlist by filter.fieldId while the executor evaluates filter.fieldName when it is present (a registry column of any registry table, qualified or not), so a filter can name columns the route refuses as fields (claims.member_id, claims.assigned_to, organization_members.role, dues_assignments.amount) with the operators in and between that both layers accept, and use the row count and the selected rows as a test of what those columns hold; the route also never reads joins, having, limit, offset or the table qualifier of a selected field, and the executor accepts limit and offset from the caller (default 1000, no maximum), so one request can ask for an unbounded read and the rate limit of 30 per hour is the only bound.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The route kept its own table allowlist, different from the registry the builder and executor use. It now validates against the executor's registry only, so one list governs data sources, fields, filters, joins, having and limits (the executor already resolved and bounded those). The route test mock now uses the real registry.

records.title: POST /api/reports/execute accepts the filter operators equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than, less_than, between and in, while the executor implements eq, ne, gt, lt, gte, lte, like, ilike, in, not_in, is_null, is_not_null and between and skips any other operator without an error: a filter with equals, not_equals, contains, greater_than or less_than passes the route, is dropped by the executor, and the report is returned with its other conditions and no restriction from that filter, so a report configured for one status, type or period returns every claim or member row of the organization (up to the limit) with success true.

POST /api/reports/execute answers 200 with success false, no data and no row count when the executor fails (an unknown data source of the executor registry, a field or column the table does not have, a join the executor refuses or a database error), because the executor returns the failure as a value and the route copies only success, data, rowCount and executionTime, dropping the error text; the audit event of that run is logged with the event type success and the success flag in its details, an exception is logged as auth_failed with severity high, and a data source the route allowlist accepts but the executor registry does not (members, deadlines, grievances) fails this way for every caller.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The executor reports a refused configuration (kind invalid) separately from a failed query (kind failed). The route answers 400 with the reason or 500, audits a validation failure or a failure, and never records an unsuccessful run as success or as an authentication failure. A database error message is no longer returned. Two executor tests that asserted the database message was returned were changed to assert it is not.

records.title: POST /api/reports/execute returns the rows of the executed configuration to any caller whose role title is officer or above: the allowlist lets the caller select the email and status of every member of the organization (and claim numbers, types, statuses and dates of every claim), with no per-field authority, no classification or consent check, no row cap smaller than the caller limit and no suppression of small groups, and the only records are a logger line by logApiAuditEvent (user, data source, counts, no rows, no field list) and the generic wrapper record of the path, so what an officer extracted is not durably recorded and no institutional decision names the offices that may reproduce member or claim columns in a report.

GET /api/reports/datasources advertises four sources (claims, organization_members, claim_deadlines, dues_assignments) with fields that the execute route does not match: the route allowlist refuses claim_deadlines and dues_assignments (400) and accepts members, deadlines and grievances that the executor registry does not have, and the registry names columns that the tables do not define (organization_members first_name and last_name where the table has name, claims outcome where the table has resolution_outcome, claim_deadlines current_deadline where the table has due_date and original_deadline), so a report built from the registry as advertised is refused by the route or fails in the database and is answered 200 with success false.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The registry named columns the tables do not have (claims.outcome, members first_name/last_name, deadlines current_deadline) and a joinable table that is not a source (claim_notes). They now map to the physical columns (resolution_outcome, due_date), the member name is the single field name, and a new ratchet fails if a registry column is not a physical column of its table. A saved report that named first_name or last_name is refused rather than run against a missing column.

records.title: GET /api/reports/datasources is wrapped in withApiAuth only and applies no role floor: any signed-in user with an organization receives the whole registry (table names, column names, types and the joinable tables, including member email, member id and dues amount columns) although running a report needs the officer role, and the organization it checks is the one on the user object, not one resolved for the query; the response contains no rows.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The registry is served at the officer floor, the same floor that can execute a report over it.

records.title: The signature request route reads the signers list from a multipart field with JSON.parse and no schema, and stores each signer name, e-mail address and user id exactly as the sender typed them, with no check that the user id belongs to the organization or to a person whose name or e-mail address matches; recordSignature then binds a signature only by requiring the signer row user id to equal the authenticated caller, so a sender can list their own user id with another person name and e-mail address, record the signature as that person (the audit trail row names the stored signer name and the sender-typed e-mail address as the actor), and when every signer row is signed the document is set to completed with no provider acknowledgment; the same local signing can complete a document that was sent through DocuSign or HelloSign without that provider ever being asked, so a signed or completed record states an identity and an act that no identified counterpart gave.

remaining: Signature bound to the document hash and provider acknowledgement, sealed audit trail, trusted-edge network evidence, signature image source: open

records.title: The signature audit trail rows are plain inserts into signature_audit_trail: the hash_chain column is declared as a future link and AuditTrailService.log never sets it, nothing recomputes the stored file hash after creation or compares it at signing or completion, no row is signed or sealed, and the signer IP address comes from the first value of a client-supplied x-forwarded-for header, the geolocation from the request body and the signature image from any URL the signer posts; the audit route nevertheless returns the rows and, with format=report, a report that the service documents as generated for legal compliance, so a document status, a report and an audit trail are presented as evidence of an e-signature when none of their contents is verified or tamper-evident.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The audit report no longer reads as certified evidence: it carries an integrity block stating the trail is unsealed, not hash-chained and not tamper-evident.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: No hash chain, file-hash recomputation at signing, or sealing is implemented, and the signer address still comes from a client-supplied forwarded header.

records.title: The void path calls provider.voidEnvelope inside a try block whose catch is empty, before and outside the transaction that records the void, and then sets the document to voided and writes the document_voided audit row and the atomic audit row whether or not the provider voided the envelope; a DocuSign or HelloSign envelope that failed to void stays open and signable by its signers at the provider while the organization record, the audit trail and the PATCH response say voided, and the provider status sync then ignores the provider later reporting completed because a voided state is final.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: A provider failure while voiding is no longer swallowed: the document is not recorded as voided and no void is audited, and the sender is told with a conflict, because the envelope can still be signed at the provider.

records.title: The signature request route has no role floor, no rate limit, no file size or type bound and no approval step: any authenticated user with an organization uploads a file in a multipart form, supplies a title, a description and a list of signers by name and e-mail address, and the service sends the file bytes, the signer names and e-mail addresses, the subject and the message to DocuSign or HelloSign under the organization provider credential, which then e-mails the typed addresses from the organization account, with no consent record for the recipients and no decision naming who may send documents for signature in the union name.

remaining: No approval step and no rate limit; the offices that may send are an institutional decision     (steward floor is an engineering default)

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Sending needs a steward, bounds the upload and the signer list, and every platform signer must be an active member of the organization (upstream's change, existing tests).

records.title: When no DocuSign or HelloSign credential is configured, or the caller sends provider internal, the provider factory returns InternalSignatureProvider, whose createEnvelope fabricates an envelope id and signing URLs that the service never stores or sends, whose status read always answers sent with no signers, and whose void and reminder methods are empty; the service nevertheless inserts the document as sent, writes the document_sent audit row, and the route answers success true, so signers who are external (no user id) receive nothing and can never sign because recordSignature rejects a signer with no user id.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The built-in provider generated envelope ids and sign URLs, stored and sent nothing, and reported every envelope as sent. It is removed: the default provider is a configured DocuSign or HelloSign account or a 501, and the document route refuses any other provider name. The tests of the stub were removed and replaced by tests that there is no built-in provider and no stub fallback.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: Documents already stored with provider "internal" keep that value; their status sync reports provider_unavailable and their void is attempted against no provider.

records.title: The request route stores expiresAt, requireAuthentication and sequentialSigning on the document and the signing order on each signer, and recordSignature checks none of them: a signature is accepted after the expiry date, out of the signing order and without the authentication the sender required, and nothing sets the expired status for an internal document, so the options the sender chose and the audit text describe controls that do not operate.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: Existing implementation, verified: recordSignature refuses an expired request and enforces sequential signing order, each with a test.
engineeringCorrection.remaining: The requireAuthentication option is still stored and not enforced, and nothing sets the expired status for an internal document.

records.title: The document status GET calls getDocumentStatus, which for any document that has a provider envelope and is not completed calls the provider and then updates the document status, the signer rows and the audit trail rows (each synchronization commits its own atomic audit under the system-provider-sync actor), so a read by any signer writes rows and makes an outbound provider call on every request, while a provider outage is swallowed and the stored status is returned as current.

The access check and the reads of signature documents, signers and audit rows run through the shared db import with no tenant context and no organization predicate (verifyDocumentAccess, getDocumentStatus, getDocumentAudit and generateAuditReport look the document up by id alone), and access rests on the sender or signer relationship, where a signer user id is whatever the sender typed with no check that it belongs to the sender organization, so a user of another organization named as a signer reads the document status, every signer row and the full audit trail of the organization, and isolation of these reads is not provable from the route or the service.

The document status returns every signer row with e-mail address, IP address, user agent, geolocation, signature image URL and provider identifiers, and the audit route returns every audit row and the report with actor e-mail addresses and IP addresses, to the sender and to every signer, so each signer, including an external counterparty who has a platform account, sees the network address and location of every other signer; the projection removes storage locations and extracted text only.

engineeringCorrection.explanation: The status, the audit trail and the audit report keep every signer network address, user agent and geolocation for the sender only. A signer sees those fields only on the rows that describe themselves. Unit tests cover sender, signer and audit rows. The audit route test mock gained getDocumentSender (disclosed adaptation).
engineeringCorrection.remaining: Signer e-mail addresses are still visible to every signer, and the report actor and signer rows carry no user id, so a signer own network data is also withheld from the report.

records.title: createSignatureRequest creates the provider envelope, which e-mails the signers, and uploads the file to document storage before the transaction that inserts the document, the signer rows, the audit trail rows and the atomic audit row, with no compensation, so a failure of the insert (for example a signer user id that is not a profile) leaves a live envelope that signers can complete and a stored file with no organization record or audit row, and the atomic audit proves only the local rows.

The document PATCH declares a zod schema (_signaturesDocumentsSchema) that requires a reason and is never applied; the handler reads action and reason from the raw JSON, accepts only the action void, and stores the reason text with no length bound in the document row, the audit trail row and the audit details.

records.title: The OAuth callback and the token refresh store the provider access token and refresh token in the text columns access_token and refresh_token of social_accounts exactly as received, with no encryption, no vault reference and no column-level protection (the calendar connection capability has a token-crypto module; nothing in lib/social-media or the social routes uses one), and the Meta, LinkedIn and X authorization requests ask for page management and posting, business_management and rw_organization_admin scopes, so a database read, backup or log exposure yields working publishing and administration credentials for every connected organization account.

records.title: For an X post with media URLs the publisher checks only that the URL scheme is http or https (its comment says it validates the URL to prevent SSRF), then calls fetch(url) from the server with default redirect following, reads the whole body with arrayBuffer with no size, content type, host or address-range check, casts the response content-type header to an image or video type and uploads the bytes to the X media endpoint, so a steward can make the server request loopback, link-local, cloud metadata or private network addresses and any redirect target, and the response of whatever answers as an image or video is posted from the organization X account.

records.title: The OAuth callback is a GET that exchanges the code, calls the platform to resolve the identity, and inserts or overwrites the social_accounts row (tokens, status active) with onConflictDoUpdate, so a state-changing request is reachable by a link, and the temporary oauth cookies are cleared before the state, user and organization are compared, so any request to the callback (a forged link or a replay) destroys the pending flow of a connection that is under way; the audit is a logApiAuditEvent call after the row is committed, which writes a log line and no audit row, and the first Facebook Page or LinkedIn organization the account lists is connected without the steward choosing one.

Any steward starts the OAuth flow for the organization, and the authorization requests ask for Meta pages_manage_posts, pages_manage_engagement, instagram_content_publish and business_management and LinkedIn w_organization_social and rw_organization_admin, which exceed what posting needs and give the stored token administrative rights over the page; the same floor refreshes and disconnects accounts, and no source names the office that may connect, replace or remove the union public identity.

publishPost inserts the social_posts row after each platform call, so a database failure after a successful platform post is caught as a platform failure and the live post has no row, no audit and a failed result; per-platform failures are caught inside the operation, so the performAuditedOperation outcome record says completed even when every platform failed, and the request answers 500 with the raw platform error text in results when none succeeded but 200 with partial results when some did; the intent and outcome audit is not committed with any data row.
